frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential-access tooling and LSASS handle requests with full-access masks were performed by user pbeesly on scranton and nashua inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion (PowerShell toolkit psversion.ps1/readme.ps1 with keystroke logging, screen capture, clipboard and private-key theft).

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM/SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_ALIAS handles and HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F write came from lsass.exe as SCRANTON$ during an LSA restart; no reg save, esentutl or hive copies found.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines, or shadow-copy activity in Sysmon, Security, PowerShell or windows.other.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No SECURITY hive/Policy Secrets handle events, no reg save HKLM\SECURITY, no lsadump/secrets command lines or script blocks.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes on nashua were made by lsass.exe itself (normal cached-credential maintenance); no external cache read or mscache/DCC2 tooling observed.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync command lines or PowerShell script blocks; no directory replication abuse in available telemetry.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity in the data is the Azure Network Watcher agent's own netsh trace on scranton.dmevals.local (SYSTEM, parent NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), i.e. platform telemetry. No tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution, no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver loads (sysmon event 6 win.Image aggregation empty), no sniff/promisc command lines, and no capture-driver service installs. The real intrusion (hidden PowerShell stager, Invoke-SeaDukeStage, PsExec with plaintext creds to NASHUA, PyInstaller python.exe beaconing to 192.168.0.4:8443) is lateral movement/C2, not network sniffing.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: LSASS handle requests and SAM object access are present, but the only non-OS, non-cmdlet LSASS access is the malicious PowerShell on scranton (reported under T1056.004); the rest are OS/Azure/Defender processes and a benign Get-Process -IncludeUserName cmdlet on nashua.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No Get-Credential/Read-Host/prompt-based credential capture; the only credential object is a hardcoded PSCredential used for WebDAV exfiltration.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No IIS/wwwroot/login page writes, w3wp activity, or HTTP POSTs; zeek window does not overlap the Windows data.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: Hidden steganography-decoding PowerShell (PID 2976, pbeesly) spawned from a malicious .scr opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF full access on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16Z.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625/4771/4776-failure/4740 events in windows.security; the only 4776 is a successful validation (Error Code 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork. No lockout or failed-auth messages in windows.other.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No failed logons and no password-referencing command lines or script blocks; the single credential validation succeeded.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua with 0x1f3fff, consistent with hash extraction for offline cracking, but no cracking tools, wordlists or potfiles were found.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 failures or lockouts; 4648 events are pbeesly/PSEXESVC reuse of known credentials, and no user-list spray tooling appears in process or script-block data.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed authentication to indicate replay of stolen credential lists; credential theft on scranton/nashua was local collection (private keys, keystrokes, password-named files archived with Rar).

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card/token interception artifacts in any dataset. The 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly used by PSEXESVC.exe/svchost.exe plus routine DWM-/UMFD-/machine-account logons; 'Credential' registry hits are CredentialGuard=0 and CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service creation by services.exe; windows.other only logs 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0'. The real credential access seen is LSASS memory access (wsmprovhost.exe GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff on nashua, powershell.exe 0x1000 on scranton), which is T1003.001 rather than T1111.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton) probed 192.168.0.4 on SMB 445/139 (all REJ), then used the Windows WebDAV redirector (DavClnt / Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362) to issue OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PROPPATCH/PUT/LOCK against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, repeatedly receiving 401 Unauthorized and re-authenticating - the classic forced-authentication/NTLM-coercion pattern - and uploaded ~2.1 MB to the remote WebDAV share (PUT 201/204). The same source 10.0.1.4 subsequently authenticated as pbeesly and SCRANTON$ to SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$ on newyork and nashua, showing use of the obtained credentials.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Two independent lsass accesses with near-full rights (0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF) came from attacker-controlled PowerShell: a hidden, execution-policy-bypass steganographic stager spawned by control.exe on scranton (PID 2976, user pbeesly), and a WMI remote-exec host wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (PID 7720, user pbeesly). Both call traces end in UNKNOWN/injected code rather than LSA modules, consistent with in-memory credential theft from lsass. Remaining lsass accesses (svchost via lsm.dll, AV, Azure telemetry, boot-time wininit/csrss) are benign.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: accesschk passwordsDB and credential file collection.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Plaintext password on PsExec64 command line.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All registry Password/Credential value sets came from svchost.exe, lsass.exe, services.exe and winlogon.exe performing normal Windows/IdentityCRL/CredentialGuard/service operations; no credential harvesting in the registry beyond the accesschk LSA read reported under T1552.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No process command line or file-access event referencing consolehost_history or other shell history files was returned in the sysmon or security datasets.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Private keys exported to .pfx and staged in 7z.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: Zeek smb_files shows only routine SYSVOL gpt.ini and GptTmpl.inf reads by two hosts during Group Policy processing; no Groups.xml/Services.xml cpassword access, and the zeek window does not overlap the Windows telemetry.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: Credential stores targeted via LSASS and browser access.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: Edge processes opened with full access on nashua.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No vaultcmd/cmdkey/DPAPI/Credential Manager activity; LSASS handle stacking shows only svchost, Azure antimalware/telemetry, Defender and boot-time system processes.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass processes, files, handles, command lines or messages in any dataset.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: 326 LSASS handle events are 293x 0x1000 from svchost.exe/Azure agents; rare high masks trace to lsm.dll, basesrv/CSRSRV and sysmain.dll. No registry, command-line or script-block evidence of authentication-process modification.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: Type-3 logons are NEWYORK$ machine-account traffic; 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly -> NASHUA and PSEXESVC on nashua using pbeesly's own credentials (PsExec), not injected credentials.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/Password registry write, no PasswordFilter command line or script block, no System32 .dll creation; only service installs are PSEXESVC and javamtsup.exe.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739, no Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod command lines or script blocks; only built-in AD module help text on newyork.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136/4738; Authentication registry writes are LogonUI session bookkeeping and CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service keys.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory changes and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD script blocks; dsregcmd.exe only loaded cryptdll.dll.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry writes or New-ItemProperty script blocks; credential-path registry writes are MuiCache and Winlogon PasswordExpiryNotification.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning found. Network-related hits were benign (Azure NetworkWatcher netsh trace, DHCP client svchost). The malicious activity present is PsExec lateral movement with plaintext credentials, a different technique.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay: WPAD lookups NXDOMAIN, NetBIOS broadcasts normal, SMB sessions Kerberos/GSSAPI-authenticated to the DC and 10.0.1.6; zero PowerShell hits for responder/mitm/llmnr/nbt-ns and no DNSClient registry change.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No ARP poisoning: MAC/IP pairings consistent per host, 12:34:56:78:9a:bc is a synthetic capture-environment MAC, no MAC claiming multiple IPs, no arp/netsh interface commands executed.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP spoofing: no DHCP event codes in windows.other, no dhcp log type in Zeek, no UDP 67/68 connections, no Dhcp references in PowerShell; only the legitimate DHCP client service.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff (full access) at 03:05:16Z inside a hidden, IEX-decoded intrusion session, and krbtgt service tickets were requested for pbeesly and SCRANTON$ on the DC newyork.dmevals.local.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4769 tickets are AES256 (0x12) with Status 0x0; no RC4 downgrade, no forged-principal 4672 logons, no golden-ticket tooling in script blocks.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: TGS requests are for machine accounts and krbtgt only, all AES256 and successful; no silver-ticket/SPN abuse indicators.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No Kerberoast/Rubeus script blocks and no RC4 service-ticket requests for user SPNs.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: Zeek kerberos shows KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED followed by successful AES256 AS exchanges, i.e. pre-auth enforced; no AS-REP roasting tooling.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: Malicious credential access on scranton.dmevals.local (PowerShell full-access LSASS open 0x1FFFFF, certificate/private-key export to .pfx, keystroke and clipboard capture, staging archive) provides the material for forging web credentials, but no forged credential was observed being created or used.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: No forged or injected web cookie activity: the only cookie-path file event is a benign svchost INetCookies write, and no cookie/session strings appear in PowerShell script blocks or Zeek HTTP.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML assertion, token or ADFS traffic in any dataset; certificate/private-key export on scranton is a plausible precursor but token forgery itself was not observed.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA/2FA/authenticator/push activity in any dataset: windows.security has zero 4625 failures and no MFA-related logon process names; PowerShell 4104 blocks contain no MFA/2FA/authenticator content (only a PowerShellGet resource string); Sysmon process creations contain no login/auth/mfa command lines; zeek HTTP has no login/auth/mfa URLs. The 85 windows.other hits are routine WMI provider starts (5857) and RSoP DeleteInstance events (5858), and the only authentication events are a single successful NTLM network logon and a RemoteInteractive logon for pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local.

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

findings.title: LSASS memory opened with full-access masks by attacker PowerShell session (pbeesly) on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 (UTC) the user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local requested handles to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe from powershell.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (DELETE, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, VM operation, read/write process memory, duplicate handle, create thread). Sysmon corroborates the same opens from PowerShell.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16.623/03:05:16.654. At 03:09:29 the same user, via a remote PowerShell session (wsmprovhost.exe, logon 0x85AAD2) on nashua.dmevals.local, again opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff. This occurred inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion: the same pbeesly session had just run a PowerShell toolkit (readme.ps1 / psversion.ps1 from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite) containing Keystroke-Check, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Clipboard, Get-PrivateKeys and Invoke-Exfil, and had executed accesschk.exe. No lsass.dmp file was written to disk in the observed window, but the access masks are those of a memory-read/credential-dump attempt against LSASS. Other LSASS opens in the dataset (svchost.exe 0x1000/0x1400, CollectGuestLogs.exe, MsMpEng.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe, wininit/csrss at process start) are normal system behaviour.
On nashua, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (PyInstaller, parent PSEXESVC.exe, pbeesly) opened lsass 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 then beaconed to 192.168.0.4:8443 from 03:15:05.

findings.title: WebDAV forced authentication from scranton (10.0.1.4) to attacker-style WebDAV server 192.168.0.4, followed by SMB/ADMIN$ credential use against nashua and newyork
findings.summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local, per the zeek-scranton log source) first probed 192.168.0.4 on TCP 445 and 139 (all connections REJ, i.e. SMB blocked), then immediately pivoted to HTTP/80 WebDAV against the same host. The client used the Windows WebDAV redirector user agents 'DavClnt' and 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and issued OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, PUT, LOCK and UNLOCK against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The server repeatedly answered 401 Unauthorized and the client re-sent the requests, which is the classic forced-authentication/NTLM-coercion pattern: the victim is made to authenticate to an attacker-controlled WebDAV endpoint so its Net-NTLM hash can be captured. The same host then wrote a file to the remote WebDAV share (PUT /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z returned 201 Created, then 204 No Content, with a 2.1 MB upload on the port-80 connection), consistent with staging data to the attacker's server. In the Windows telemetry window (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28 UTC, non-overlapping with zeek) the same source address 10.0.1.4 is seen authenticating as user 'pbeesly' and as machine account 'SCRANTON$' to SYSVOL, IPC$ and ADMIN$ shares on newyork.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local (9 ADMIN$ accesses to \\*\ADMIN$ -> \??\C:\windows on nashua between 23:10 and 23:18 local time), i.e. the coerced/obtained credentials were used for lateral SMB access. The SMB connections observed in Sysmon to 10.0.0.4 and 10.0.1.6 are System-process (port 445/139) domain traffic and are not themselves coercive, but the WebDAV sequence is a clear forced-authentication attempt.

findings.title: Hidden PowerShell stager (control.exe parent) opened lsass with full-access 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PID 2976 (C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, IntegrityLevel High) was spawned at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z by C:\Windows\System32\control.exe with the command line "PowerShell.exe" -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden -c "sal a New-Object;Add-Type -AssemblyName 'System.Drawing'; $g=a System.Drawing.Bitmap('C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png');...IEX([System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($o[0..3932]))" — a steganographic, hidden-window, execution-policy-bypass loader. At 03:05:16Z that same process (SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, i.e. PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-equivalent rights that permit reading credential material. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), not a Windows LSA module, indicating code injected/allocated in the PowerShell process rather than a legitimate LSA API path. This is the only PowerShell-to-lsass full-access pair in the dataset and is consistent with in-memory credential theft from lsass.

findings.title: Credential theft and certificate/private-key export by PowerShell on SCRANTON (pbeesly) — no forged web credential observed
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell session (PID 2976, launched 02:58:44 from control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden and an IEX-decoded bitmap payload) that performed credential access: at 03:04:56 it defined and ran Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports each certificate with a thumbprint to a random .pfx file in the user's Downloads folder (coyn5igj.3io.pfx created 03:04:57); at 03:05:16 the same PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access, call trace ending in an UNKNOWN module) and again with 0x1f3fff; it then ran screen capture (gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp, 03:06:00), Get-Clipboard, Get-Keystrokes, and staged an archive at C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\OfficeSupplies.7z (03:08:35) with a cleanup function that deletes *.pfx/*.bmp/*.png and OfficeSupplies.7z. It then moved laterally to NASHUA with Invoke-Command and PsExec64 using the cleartext password for dmevals\pbeesly, producing 4648 explicit-credential logons on scranton (10.0.1.6) and PSEXESVC.exe logons on nashua. The stolen material (exported private keys/certificates, LSASS memory, keystrokes, clipboard) is the raw material for forging web credentials, but no forged cookie or SAML assertion was observed being used: no cookie/SAML/token strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, no SAML/ADFS/token URLs in Zeek HTTP, and the only cookie-path file event is a benign svchost INetCookies write. The technique family is therefore assessed as malicious credential access on the host, with the forging step itself not observed.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on scranton.dmevals.local
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) executed a staged PowerShell chain: at 2020-05-01T23:03:49-04:00 'Move-Item .\readme.txt readme.ps1' renamed a file to a .ps1, at 23:03:57 '. .\readme.ps1' dot-sourced it, and at 23:04:56 the function 'Get-PrivateKeys' was defined and invoked. The script block (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded plaintext password 'saribas'. At 2020-05-02T03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876), and at 03:04:57.272-03:04:57.428Z the same powershell.exe (PID 3876) wrote certificate store blobs under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646\Blob and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob. This is theft of authentication certificates (including private keys) for later use/forgery. The other certificate-store registry writes in the window (lsass.exe, svchost.exe, smss.exe, taskhostw.exe, and the single 4657 on nashua.dmevals.local by NASHUA$ via C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe) are routine OS certificate-store maintenance and are not attacker activity.

findings.title: LSASS accessed with full access by PowerShell on scranton, but no cracking artifacts
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16.654Z the process C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff, and a second handle with 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16.623Z; wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local also opened lsass with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29.430Z. These are the only non-system, non-Azure-agent LSASS accesses with read/full masks (the 289 svchost.exe accesses are 0x1000 only). This is consistent with in-memory credential theft feeding offline cracking, but no cracking tooling, wordlists, potfiles or hash-conversion script blocks were found, so T1110.002 (password cracking) itself is not evidenced.

On scranton.dmevals.local, in the same session where user pbeesly ran a hidden, encoded PowerShell stager (monkey.png bitmap-decoded IEX launched from control.exe at 02:58:44), a PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976) opened the Microsoft Edge browser process (PID 7748, C:\Windows\SystemApps\Microsoft.MicrosoftEdge_8wekyb3d8bbwe\MicrosoftEdge.exe) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:17Z, and immediately afterwards opened MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe and MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe with the same full access. Full-process access to a browser is the prerequisite for reading session cookies out of browser memory. No cookie file access, cookie-named command line, or cookie-related script block was observed, so the theft itself is not proven; the surrounding activity (hidden encoded PowerShell, credential-file harvesting script, PsExec, sdelete) makes this access suspicious rather than benign.

findings.title: No SAML token forgery observed; certificate/private-key export is the closest precursor
findings.summary: No SAML assertion, NotOnOrAfter or Assertion strings appear in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, no process command line references saml/token/cert, and no Zeek HTTP request targets saml/adfs/token URLs. However, on scranton.dmevals.local the attacker-run PowerShell executed Get-PrivateKeys at 03:04:56, exporting every LocalMachine certificate with a thumbprint to random .pfx files (coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57) using the hardcoded password 'saribas' — private keys and certificates are exactly the material used to sign forged SAML tokens, so this is a plausible precursor, but the forging/use of a token itself was not observed in these datasets.

findings.title: SAM database and SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_SERVER handles opened by lsass.exe on scranton (system-account context, no attacker tooling)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:19:10-23:19:22 (local, = 03:19 UTC) lsass.exe running as SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3E7) requested handles to SAM_SERVER 'SAM' (0xf003f), SAM_DOMAIN 'SCRANTON' (0xf07df) and SAM_ALIAS 'DOMAINS\Builtin\Aliases\00000221' (0xf), and wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F. This is the local LSA/SAM service itself, not an external dumping tool: no reg save of HKLM\SAM/SECURITY, no esentutl/ntdsutil, and no SAM/SECURITY hive file copies were found (the only file-create hits matching SAM/SECURITY were Prefetch .pf files). The SAM access coincides with an lsass.exe restart on the host (lsass.exe process create at 03:19:09.809, LsaPid write 0x2ec, CredentialGuard Enabled=0), i.e. normal LSA initialization. No evidence of an adversary extracting local account hashes.

findings.title: No NTDS.dit / volume-shadow / ntdsutil activity observed
findings.summary: Searches for NTDS file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines in Sysmon and Security 4688, and for shadow/VSS/ntds strings in windows.other and PowerShell script blocks returned no hits. The only domain-controller-like host in scope (newyork) shows only routine service activity (UsoClient, dsregcmd, W32Time). No evidence of NTDS extraction.

findings.title: No LSA Secrets / SECURITY hive dumping observed
findings.summary: No process creations with secrets/lsadump/reg save HKLM\SECURITY, no 4656/4663/4670 events on SECURITY Policy Secrets objects, and no PowerShell or windows.other messages referencing LSA secrets were found. The only SECURITY-related registry activity was lsass.exe writing HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua (see T1003.005).

findings.title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes by lsass.exe on nashua — normal cached-credential maintenance, not dumping
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 728) set the value HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 to 'Binary Data' at 03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49 and 03:15:03 on 2020-05-02. These are writes by the LSA process itself to the cached-domain-credential cache, consistent with normal logon/cache updates (the same host was being accessed by pbeesly around this time), not an external read of the cache. No security-audit handle events on SECURITY\Cache objects and no PowerShell referencing mscache/DCC2 were found, so there is no evidence of cached credential extraction.

findings.title: No DCSync / DRSUAPI replication abuse observed
findings.summary: No process command lines containing drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync and no PowerShell script blocks referencing DCSync/lsadump/drsuapi were found. The attacker's PowerShell activity on scranton/nashua focused on keystroke logging, screen capture, clipboard, private-key export and exfiltration, plus PsExec to NASHUA with plaintext credentials, but no directory replication request was observed in the available telemetry.

findings.title: Azure Network Watcher agent performs netsh packet capture on SCRANTON (platform telemetry, not adversary sniffing)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z, netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (LogonId 0x3e7, session 0) with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and stopped at 03:19:24Z with 'netsh trace stop'. The parent is the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service (C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), which was itself installed/started as a service on the same host minutes earlier (4688 'Install /service /autoStart', 'Test /service /autoStart', '/service'). This is the Azure platform's own packet-capture capability, not attacker-driven sniffing: no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver load, no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution, and no sniff/promiscuous command lines were found anywhere in the Windows telemetry.

findings.title: No adversary network-sniffing tooling observed; the real intrusion on NASHUA used a PyInstaller python.exe beacon, not a sniffer
findings.summary: Hunting for T1040-specific artifacts across windows.sysmon, windows.security and windows.powershell returned nothing: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap process creation, no pcap/npcap/winpcap image loads (sysmon event 6 aggregation on win.Image returned 0 buckets), no sniff/promisc/pcap command lines, and no capture-driver service installs (the only 7045 services were a Java support service and PSEXESVC). The genuine compromise in this window is separate from sniffing: on scranton.dmevals.local user pbeesly ran a hidden, encoded PowerShell stager (monkey.png bitmap decode + IEX), then 'Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA' and repeated PsExec64 with plaintext credentials (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), which spawned PSEXESVC and C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (SHA256 43782EC4337D8F3DDB7EA0C451B3BC4F212F84C8D5571BD0A842001C859A02AE) that unpacked a PyInstaller bundle to _MEI29522 and opened many TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. That is C2/lateral movement, not passive network sniffing, so T1040 is not supported by the evidence.

findings.title: LSASS handle requests and SAM object access on scranton/nashua are OS-internal or benign PowerShell cmdlet activity
findings.summary: The 4656 handle-request hits to lsass.exe/SAM are dominated by legitimate system activity: lsass.exe itself opening SAM_SERVER (AccessMask 0xf003f, subject SCRANTON$ logon 0x3E7), Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe, Azure CollectGuestLogs.exe, and svchost.exe. The one non-OS LSASS open outside scranton's malicious PowerShell was wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z with 0x1F3FFF, but its call trace runs through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll and coincides with the benign script block 'Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Select-Object UserName,SessionId' at 03:09:28-29Z, i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet enumerating process owners rather than credential theft. The remaining LSASS opens (svchost 0x1000 x286, AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400) are standard.

findings.title: Routine domain SMB/SYSVOL/IPC$ share access and System-process SMB connections are benign background activity
findings.summary: The bulk of the T1187 check hits are normal domain operations, not forced authentication. Of 163 share-access events (5140/5145), the shares are only \\*\SYSVOL (69), \\*\IPC$ (65) and \\*\ADMIN$ (29) - standard Group Policy replication and remote-management shares. Many are machine-account authentications (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$) over IPv6 link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 or from 10.0.1.4, matching DFSR/GPO traffic. The 66 Sysmon event.code 3 hits on ports 445/139 all come from process.executable 'System' (PID 4) to 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and the local link-local address, i.e. kernel SMB client/server traffic, not a user-mode coercer. The 1649 Sysmon file-creation events are dominated by prefetch, EventLog lastalive*.dat, DFSR replica XML, GroupPolicy DataStore and Cortana cache files - no .lnk/.scf/.url/.library-ms coercion files were observed. Zeek SMB connections (45 to 445, 5 to 139) are internal host-to-host traffic. The PowerShell (4104) and windows.other checks for 445/WebDAV/NTLM returned zero hits. Only the 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4 WebDAV sequence is anomalous; the remaining share and SMB activity is consistent with normal AD administration.

findings.title: Remaining lsass process-access events are legitimate Windows LSA/AV/telemetry behaviour
findings.summary: Of 326 Sysmon event-10 accesses to lsass.exe, 289 come from svchost.exe and the rest from AntimalwareConfig.exe (15), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13), wininit.exe (2), csrss.exe (1) and services.exe (1) — normal LSA, AV and Azure guest-agent activity. The rare masks are also benign: the svchost 0x101001 access on scranton at 03:18:34Z has a call trace entirely through c:\windows\system32\lsm.dll (the LSA policy provider), and the wininit/csrss 0x1FFFFF/0x1000000 accesses at 03:19:09Z are the standard boot-time lsass initialisation by its parent processes. The two PowerShell 0x1000 accesses (read-only, VM_READ) are not credential-dumping rights. No exploit artefacts were found in windows.other (no 'exploit' messages) or in PowerShell script blocks (no Invoke-*/Exploit matches), and the Zeek notices/weirds are from a non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window with no credential-access content.

The remaining T1539 hits are normal Windows behaviour: (1) svchost.exe (SYSTEM) created C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\warp_jit_...\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:21:05Z, a WARP/AppContainer cookie store file, not a browser profile cookie DB; (2) five 4688 events on scranton.dmevals.local show rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav under pbeesly — the WebDAV client setting a cookie for a WebDAV share, not theft; (3) the bulk of Edge process-access events (Sysmon 10) come from Explorer.EXE (0x2000) and svchost.exe/sysmain (0x3000) on scranton and nashua, i.e. shell and prefetch/superfetch activity. No cookie database file access, no cookie-related script block (4104) and no cookie-related windows.other message was found.
findings.title: Benign browser cookie-store and cookie-URL artifacts (INetCookies file creation, davclnt DavSetCookie, Edge memory access by Explorer/svchost)
Registry Password/Credential value sets are Windows service and identity-provider noise
findings.summary: The 17 Sysmon 13 hits on registry paths containing Password/Credential are all written by legitimate system processes: svchost.exe setting HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength / ProviderPasswordCharacterGroups on nashua and scranton, lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0 on scranton, services.exe creating the CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service values, and winlogon.exe writing PasswordExpiryNotification\NotShownTime. None of these are credential harvesting; the only genuine registry credential access observed is accesschk.exe reading the LSA key, reported under T1552.

findings.title: SYSVOL GptTmpl.inf / gpt.ini reads are routine Group Policy processing, not GPP credential harvesting
findings.summary: Zeek smb_files shows two hosts (simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan 10.0.1.4 at 2020-04-30T00:12:01Z and bobs.bigwheel.local 10.0.1.6 at 00:20:49Z) opening \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol paths gpt.ini, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf and the policy folder tree. These are the standard files a domain member reads during Group Policy refresh; no Groups.xml, Services.xml or ScheduledTasks.xml with cpassword was accessed, and the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows host telemetry (2020-05-02). No GPP-embedded credential access is evidenced.

findings.title: LSASS handle activity is dominated by Windows/Azure components; no Credential Manager (vault/cmdkey/DPAPI) access
findings.summary: Stacking all 326 Sysmon EID 10 events targeting lsass.exe shows the bulk is routine: svchost.exe 0x1000 (286 events), Microsoft Azure IaaSAntimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe 0x1400 (13), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400 (11), svchost 0x101001 (2, lsm.dll call trace), svchost 0x3000 (1, sysmain.dll), and boot-time wininit/csrss 0x1fffff/0x1000000. Security object-access auditing on lsass.exe likewise shows only CollectGuestLogs.exe (0x1410/0x10), MsMpEng.exe (0x1fffff/0x10) and lsass itself (0x1478). No vaultcmd, cmdkey, DPAPI, Credential Manager registry/file access, or 4688/4104 command lines referencing vault or credentials were found; the only 'Credential' message is a routine Credential Guard configuration event (0x0) on scranton. The two anomalous PowerShell/wsmprovhost LSASS handles are reported under T1555.

findings.title: LSASS handle access on all four hosts is dominated by svchost.exe with benign access masks; no authentication-process modification observed
findings.summary: 326 Sysmon event.code 10 accesses to lsass.exe were recorded between 2020-05-02T02:56 and 03:28. Stacking by source image gives svchost.exe 289 (scranton 219, newyork 30, nashua 28, utica 12), AntimalwareConfig.exe 15, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 13, PowerShell.exe/powershell.exe 4, wininit.exe 2, csrss.exe 1, services.exe 1, wsmprovhost.exe 1. Stacking by GrantedAccess shows 293 of 326 are 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION). The rare high masks are all explained by their call traces: svchost.exe 0x101001 at 03:18:34 on scranton comes through lsm.dll (Local Session Manager), wininit.exe/csrss.exe 0x1fffff at 03:19:09 on scranton come through wininit.exe/basesrv.DLL/CSRSRV.dll (session teardown/restart), and svchost.exe 0x3000 at 03:19:59 comes through sysmain.dll. The only PowerShell full-access handle (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16 on scranton, PID 2976) has an UNKNOWN call trace, but the surrounding PowerShell 4104/4103 records for that window show only screen-capture code (Invoke-ScreenCapture, Add-Type System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing, Start-Job 'Screenshot'), not credential access. No 4657 registry write to LSA/SAM/cryptdll/msv1_0, no 4688 command line referencing lsass/cryptdll/msv1_0, and no PowerShell script block referencing lsass/cryptdll/msv1_0 was found.

findings.title: Network logons are machine-account and PsExec traffic; no DC authentication backdoor
findings.summary: 218 type-3 logons (4624) are dominated by the NEWYORK$ machine account from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 and 10.0.0.4 on newyork.dmevals.local, i.e. normal machine-account network authentication. The 15 explicit-credential logons (4648) show user pbeesly authenticating to target server NASHUA from scranton.dmevals.local (source 10.0.1.6) and, on nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe using pbeesly's own credentials against localhost — consistent with PsExec lateral movement, not with injected/false credentials. No 4657 write to LSA/SAM/cryptdll/msv1_0 and no lsass/cryptdll reference in windows.other or PowerShell script blocks was found.

findings.title: No password filter DLL registration or System32 DLL drop
findings.summary: No 4657 registry write to Notification Packages/Password/lsass, no 4688 command line containing Notification or PasswordFilter, no PowerShell script block containing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsass, and no Sysmon event.code 11 file creation of a .dll under System32 were returned. The only service installs in windows.other are PSEXESVC (%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, demand start, four times on nashua.dmevals.local by pbeesly) and 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe, auto start, on scranton.dmevals.local) — neither is a password filter package.

findings.title: No reversible-encryption or AD account-flag modification
findings.summary: No 4739 (domain policy change), no 4688/Sysmon event.code 1 command line containing Reversible/Set-ADUser/dsmod, no PowerShell 4104/4103 referencing AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption, and no windows.other message referencing Reversible were returned. The only AD-related PowerShell content on newyork.dmevals.local is the built-in ActiveDirectory module resource/help text (MSFT_ScriptResourceStrings.psd1, Get-CommonADParameters help), not a user-flag change.

findings.summary: No 5136 directory-service change events were returned in windows.security or windows.other, and no PowerShell script block containing Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD was found. The only hybrid-identity-adjacent activity is dsregcmd.exe on newyork.dmevals.local loading cryptdll.dll at 03:06:14, which is the standard device-registration client loading the crypto manager DLL.

findings.title: No Network Provider DLL registration
findings.summary: No 4657 write to NetworkProvider/Credential-related registry keys and no PowerShell script block containing NetworkProvider/New-ItemProperty were returned. The registry writes touching credential-related paths on scranton.dmevals.local are MuiCache entries for CredentialEnrollmentManager.exe written by services.exe and the Winlogon PasswordExpiryNotification values written by winlogon.exe — standard OS behaviour, not a network provider DLL registration.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity; observed credential theft is PsExec lateral movement with plaintext credentials
findings.summary: Hunting for AiTM positioning (rogue SMB/relay hosts, name-resolution anomalies, network tampering) produced no attacker-in-the-middle evidence in any dataset. The real malicious activity in the Windows window is different: user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran PsExec64.exe from PowerShell four times (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42) against \\NASHUA with the password supplied in cleartext on the command line, staging C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local via ADMIN$ (5145 at 03:10:23) and installing PSEXESVC (4697/7045) four times. That is lateral movement / credential misuse, not AiTM. The only 'network' hits were benign: netsh.exe trace start/stop spawned by the Azure NetworkWatcherAgent, and svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p -s Dhcp (the DHCP client service).

findings.title: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay; SMB traffic is normal domain authentication
findings.summary: Name-resolution and SMB activity in the Zeek capture (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) shows only ordinary domain behaviour: wpad.dmevals.local lookups returning NXDOMAIN every ~10 minutes from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6, NetBIOS broadcast lookups for SCRANTON/NASHUA to 10.0.1.255, and LDAP/Kerberos SRV queries against the DC 10.0.0.4. SMB sessions are Kerberos/GSSAPI-authenticated to the DC (10.0.0.4) and to 10.0.1.6, with no unauthenticated relay-style SMB to an unexpected host. No PowerShell script block referenced responder, mitm, llmnr or nbt-ns (zero hits), and no 4657 registry change to DNSClient was recorded. The 4697 service installs in the Windows window are PSEXESVC (lateral movement) and Windows per-user services, not relay tooling.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC/IP pairings are consistent per host
findings.summary: Stacking L2 addresses on Zeek conn records shows three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and responder MACs 12:34:56:78:9a:bc plus broadcast ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. The 12:34:56:78:9a:bc value is a synthetic/placeholder MAC used by the capture environment, not a rogue device claiming multiple IPs. The 00:35:26 flows from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 on 445 are recorded by the second sensor (bobs.bigwheel.local) with that sensor's own view of the same hosts, and no single MAC is seen claiming multiple distinct IPs in a way that indicates gratuitous ARP poisoning. No PowerShell script block referenced arp or netsh interface (zero hits), and no netsh interface/ARP manipulation command was executed on any host.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; DHCP traffic is the local client service only
findings.summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the collected data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP server/client event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits), the Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type at all (only conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, dpd, smb_files, weird, smb_mapping, notice, pe), and no PowerShell script block mentioned Dhcp. Sysmon network connections show no traffic to UDP 67/68; the only DHCP-related process is the legitimate svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p -s Dhcp client service on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19:11.

findings.title: No golden-ticket evidence: krbtgt TGS requests are AES256 and no forged-ticket indicators
findings.summary: All 28 4769 events on newyork.dmevals.local have TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and Status 0x0; the krbtgt service-ticket requests by pbeesly (03:04:04Z) and SCRANTON$ (03:19:13Z, 03:19:15Z) are ordinary TGS requests with no RC4 downgrade, no anomalous principals and no 4672 special-privilege logons attributable to a forged principal (the 4672 aggregation returned no buckets). No golden-ticket forging is observable; the LSASS access is reported under T1558 as credential theft.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators in TGS requests
findings.summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local are for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all AES256 (0x12) with Status 0x0 and normal ticket options; no service-account SPN ticket burst or RC4 service ticket typical of silver-ticket use was observed. No PowerShell script block referenced silver tickets or SPNs.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting observed
findings.summary: No PowerShell script block contained Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus strings, and the 4769 stack shows only AES256 tickets for machine accounts and krbtgt — no RC4 (0x17) service-ticket requests for user SPNs that would indicate Kerberoasting. The credential theft on scranton targeted LSASS memory rather than service-ticket roasting.

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting observed
findings.summary: Zeek kerberos records (2020-04-30 window) show only pbeesly AS exchanges to krbtgt/DMEVALS.LOCAL that first return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and then succeed with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 — i.e. pre-authentication is enforced, so no AS-REP roasting. No PowerShell script block referenced AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth.

findings.title: No forged web cookies observed; only cookie-path file event is a benign svchost INetCookies write
findings.summary: The single file-creation event matching a cookie store is svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:21:05 — a normal LocalService package cache write, not browser cookie theft or injection. No PowerShell 4104 script block in the window contained cookie/Set-Cookie/session strings, and the Zeek HTTP records (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) show only 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4 requests with no cookie or session-token evidence retrievable. The credential theft on scranton (LSASS access, keystrokes, clipboard) could enable session hijacking, but no forged cookie was observed.

findings.title: No MFA/2FA request-generation activity observed; windows.other hits are routine WMI provider and RSoP events
findings.summary: The only T1621 check with hits (C355, 85 events in windows.other) consists entirely of WMI provider start events (5857, 36 events: dsccore, CIMWin32, deploymentprovider, dnsclientcim, StorageWMI, MSVDS__PROVIDER, Win32_WIN32_TERMINALSERVICE_Prov, WMIProv, BcdProv, SppProvider, all 'result code 0x0' under wmiprvse.exe) and WMI RSoP DeleteInstance events (5858, 49 events, 48 on newyork.dmevals.local with ResultCode 0x80041002 for RSOP_ExtensionStatus GUIDs). The single 5858 on scranton.dmevals.local is a WMI ExecNotificationQuery for Win32_ProcessStartTrace WHERE ProcessName = 'wsmprovhost.exe' (ResultCode 0x80041032). None of these are authentication or MFA-push events; they are normal WMI/RSoP housekeeping. No 4625 failures exist in windows.security (C352/C353 zero hits), no MFA/2FA/authenticator strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks (C354 zero; the one 'verify' match is a PowerShellGet resource-string block on scranton under user pbeesly), no login/auth/mfa command lines in Sysmon process creation (C356 zero), and no login/auth/mfa HTTP URLs in zeek (C357 zero). The only authentication activity of note is a single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2, workstation 10.0.1.4, source 172.18.39.2) for pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:20:41Z followed by a type 10 RemoteInteractive logon for the same account at 03:20:46Z — a successful logon sequence, not repeated MFA prompts or push bombing. No evidence of MFA request generation in this dataset.

findings.title: Routine certificate-store registry writes and Kerberos TGT requests (benign context)
findings.summary: The remaining T1649 check hits are normal system behaviour. The 4657 registry-modification event on nashua.dmevals.local (2020-05-01T23:16:19-04:00) was performed by machine account NASHUA$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3E7) via C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe on the ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 Blob, i.e. a certificate-store blob update, not attacker tampering. The other SystemCertificates registry writes in sysmon came from lsass.exe, svchost.exe, smss.exe and taskhostw.exe (AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS physical-store values) — standard Windows certificate propagation. The 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests on newyork.dmevals.local were for pbeesly (9) and the SCRANTON$ machine account (5) from internal addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, with no PKINIT/certificate-based anomalies visible. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net 376, conn.sons.info 2) are from a non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window and show no forged-certificate indicators. Note: the malicious certificate export itself is reported in the separate malicious finding.

incidents.title: LSASS memory access with full-access masks by attacker PowerShell on scranton and WMI/WinRM host on nashua
incidents.rationale: All four findings describe the same LSASS handle opens: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) on scranton with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z and wsmprovhost.exe/python.exe on nashua with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. F16 and F31 are alternate interpretations of the same events; F55 adds the PsExec-pushed python.exe LSASS open and beacon. This is OS credential dumping from LSASS memory (T1003.001).

incidents.title: PowerShell keystroke logger and clipboard capture on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly ran Get-Keystrokes (job 'Keystrokes') and Get-Clipboard on scranton — keylogging (T1056.001).

incidents.title: WebDAV forced authentication from scranton followed by SMB/ADMIN$ credential use against nashua and newyork
incidents.rationale: scranton (10.0.1.4) probed SMB then pivoted to WebDAV against 192.168.0.4 using DavClnt/MiniRedir user agents, followed by ADMIN$ access to nashua as pbeesly and SCRANTON$ activity on newyork — forced authentication to capture/relay credentials (T1187).

incidents.title: Steganographic hidden PowerShell stager (control.exe parent) that opened LSASS on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same process entity: the hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976) spawned by control.exe that decoded monkey.png and IEX'd the payload, then opened LSASS with full access. The credential-access action is exploitation/execution of the stager enabling credential access (T1212).

incidents.title: WMI remote-exec host opened LSASS on nashua
incidents.rationale: wsmprovhost.exe (pbeesly) created via WMI/WinRM remote execution opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF on nashua; the credential-access action is exploitation of the remote-execution channel to reach LSASS (T1212).

incidents.title: accesschk.exe credential reconnaissance creating passwordsDB and querying LSA registry key on scranton
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same accesschk.exe execution by pbeesly that created passwordsDB and queried HKLM\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa — credential hunting for unsecured credentials on the host (T1552).

incidents.title: Plaintext password on PsExec64 command line used against NASHUA
incidents.rationale: Both findings describe the same PsExec64 invocations with -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by in cleartext on the command line and in script blocks, producing 4648 logons on nashua — credentials in files/command lines (T1552.001).

incidents.title: Credential-named file collection and password-protected archive on nashua
incidents.rationale: PowerShell collected *pass*,*login*,*admin*,*vpn* files into working.zip and Rar.exe re-archived with a password, then sdelete64 wiped artifacts — searching for credentials in files (T1552.001).

incidents.title: PowerShell opened Microsoft Edge browser processes with full access on scranton
incidents.rationale: PowerShell (PID 2976) opened MicrosoftEdge.exe and its subprocesses with 0x1FFFFF during the intrusion, consistent with extracting credentials from the web browser (T1555.003).

incidents.title: Browser processes opened with full access on nashua
incidents.rationale: wsmprovhost (pbeesly) opened MicrosoftEdge.exe and MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe with 0x1f3fff on nashua, consistent with extracting credentials from the web browser (T1555.003).

incidents.title: Kerberos ticket requests for krbtgt alongside LSASS access on scranton
incidents.rationale: Full-access LSASS handles plus 4769 ticket requests for krbtgt from pbeesly on the DC indicate Kerberos ticket theft/forgery activity (T1558).

incidents.title: No SAML token forgery observed; certificate export is closest precursor
incidents.rationale: No SAML assertion or token artifacts were found; the only related activity is the private-key/certificate export, which is a precursor to forging SAML tokens (T1606.002).

incidents.title: Certificate/private-key export via Get-PrivateKeys on scranton
incidents.rationale: All three findings describe the same Get-PrivateKeys execution that enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported certificates with private keys to password-protected .pfx files (coyn5igj.3io.pfx), with F60 adding exfil staging — stealing authentication certificates (T1649).

incidents.title: In-memory DLL compilation via csc.exe on scranton
incidents.rationale: PowerShell invoked csc.exe to compile DLLs in the user Temp directory — this is obfuscated/compiled payload execution (T1027), not credential access.

incidents.title: Masqueraded .scr stager in ProgramData\victim on scranton
incidents.rationale: A masqueraded .scr launched from explorer spawned cmd/powershell to start the intrusion — this is execution/user execution (T1204), not credential access.

incidents.title: hostui.exe launched with -verb runas for elevation on scranton
incidents.rationale: PowerShell launched hostui.exe with -verb runas to force a UAC elevation prompt — privilege escalation (T1548), not credential access.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe spawned by cmd on scranton
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe, a known UAC-bypass binary, was spawned by cmd during the intrusion — privilege escalation/UAC bypass (T1548), not credential access.
